passage: Rashmi, you're leaving for Hyderabad next month, so listen to your Jeevan thatha for once. At nineteen I took the train from Mangalore to Bombay for a mill job. The first week was all noise and wonder. By the sixth week, nobody knew my name. The canteen rice was wrong, the fish was wrong, even the rain smelled wrong. I shared a room with five men from Bihar who were kind, but their jokes went over my head. At night I lay on my mat and cried into my towel so nobody would hear. I wrote to my amma that I wanted to come home. She wrote back, 'Come if you must. But wait till Deepavali first.' I waited. That crying didn't mean I had chosen wrong, kutty. It meant I loved where I came from. Both things were true.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan go at nineteen, and why?
qa.a: He took the train from Mangalore to Bombay for a mill job.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he cried into his towel?
qa.a: He was homesick and lonely, missing familiar food and being known, and felt like an outsider among kind strangers.

qa.q: What helped Jeevan through this stage?
qa.a: His amma's letter allowed him to come home but asked him to wait till Deepavali, which gave him time without shame.

qa.q: What might Jeevan's amma have felt reading his letter?
qa.a: She likely felt the ache of missing him and worry, yet chose to steady him rather than pull him straight home.

grounding: Shows homesickness and culture shock weeks after a move, with night-time crying that does not mean the move was a mistake.

passage: On Pongal night, Shankar's phone screen cracked in the tram door, and with it went his video call home. He was twenty, seven weeks into his engineering exchange in Stuttgart, and the one thing he had planned all week was watching Amma draw the kolam live. Now the screen was a black web. In the shared kitchen, his flatmate Lokesh, from Hubballi, was stirring instant noodles. 'Use my laptop,' Lokesh offered, but the Wi-Fi was down in the whole building. Shankar sat on the floor by the radiator. Nobody here knew it was a festival. Nobody knew he liked his rice with ghee. He cried quietly, and was surprised at himself. Lokesh sat down beside him with two bowls. 'Library Wi-Fi, first thing tomorrow,' he said. 'You'll see the kolam, just a day late.' Shankar nodded and ate, homesick and grateful at once.

qa.q: What ruined Shankar's plan for the video call?
qa.a: His phone screen cracked in the tram door, and the Wi-Fi was down in the whole building.

qa.q: Why was Shankar surprised at himself?
qa.a: He didn't expect to cry; the missed festival call showed how much he missed his family and being known.

qa.q: What helped at this point, and what could help next?
qa.a: Lokesh's company and the plan for library Wi-Fi eased the night; regular calls home could keep his base steady through the harder weeks.

qa.q: What might Lokesh be experiencing as he sits beside Shankar?
qa.a: Lokesh, also far from home, may recognise the feeling and want to comfort his flatmate without any fuss 🤍

grounding: Illustrates homesickness weeks into a move abroad, made sharper by a broken phone on a festival night, with crying that does not mean the move was wrong.

passage:
Lokesh, you asked why I went quiet in October. Okay. I'm Pooja, I'm from Jorhat, and for about three weeks I cried every night in the hostel bathroom with the tap running so nobody would hear.

Nothing bad happened. That was the strange part. Classes were fine. But nobody here knew me. At home, the man at the tea stall knows how I take my tea. Here I was just "the northeast girl" and people asked if I ate snakes, which, no.

I missed Ma's fish tenga so badly I actually dreamt about it. I looked at train tickets home twice. I didn't buy them.

What I figured out, slowly, is that wanting to go home didn't mean coming here was a mistake. It meant I'd left something real behind. Both things were true at once.

qa.q: Where did Pooja cry every night?
qa.a: Pooja cried in the hostel bathroom with the tap running.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling during those three weeks?
qa.a: Pooja felt homesick and lonely, like an outsider nobody knew, and sad enough to look at train tickets home twice.

qa.q: What could help someone in Pooja's place at this stage?
qa.a: Telling one trusted person, as Pooja is now telling Lokesh, and keeping a small link to home such as calls with Ma or cooking a familiar dish, can make the outsider feeling lighter.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel hearing why Pooja went quiet?
qa.a: Lokesh may feel concerned and touched to be trusted, and perhaps sorry for not noticing sooner.

grounding: A spoken account shows weeks of homesickness and feeling like an outsider, and that wanting to go home did not mean the move was wrong.

passage:
Week five, Monday: Sudha woke at 3 a.m. with her pillow damp. In the dark she whispered, "Amma," just to hear the word. In Delhi nobody made kozhukattai on Mondays. Nobody called her Sudhu.

Week five, Friday: At lunch a classmate laughed at how she said "yesterday." Sudha smiled and went back to her room and cried again, then texted Leela, her roommate, who was still at the library: "I think I want to go home. For good." Leela came back early with two samosas and sat on the floor beside her bed. "You're allowed to hate it this week," Leela said.

Week seven, Sunday: Sudha cooked sambar in the hostel kitchen, badly. Three girls from her floor ate it anyway. She still missed home. But she noticed she hadn't cried since Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Leela bring when she came back early?
qa.a: Leela came back with two samosas.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she texted that she wanted to go home for good?
qa.a: She felt homesick, hurt by the teasing and like an outsider, so much that returning home seemed the only relief.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage, and how did Leela help?
qa.a: The turning point is not deciding while at the lowest; Leela sat with her and allowed the feeling without pushing, which gave Sudha time to find small anchors like cooking sambar.

qa.q: What is it like for Leela to get that text?
qa.a: Leela was probably worried and caring, since she left the library early and simply stayed with Sudha.

grounding: Over several weeks it shows homesickness and culture shock, crying and wanting to return, without the move being wrong.

passage:
Tejas, beta, you sound like I did in 1994. Sit, let me tell you.

I came to Mumbai from Indore at nineteen for my hotel management course. Everyone here spoke fast, walked fast, ate fast. My roommate was from Goa and put vinegar in things. I didn't know one person who remembered my birthday.

The first month I was fine. The second month I cried every night into my dupatta so my roommate wouldn't hear. I wrote to my mother, "I want to come back." I posted it and then regretted it.

She wrote back: "Come if you need to. Your room is here. But give it till Diwali."

I gave it till Diwali. And your Alka aunty is still here, thirty years later. The crying didn't mean I was wrong to come. It meant I was far from everything that knew me.

qa.q: Where did Alka come from, and at what age?
qa.a: Alka came to Mumbai from Indore at nineteen.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling in her second month in Mumbai?
qa.a: She felt deeply homesick and alone, crying at night and writing to her mother that she wanted to return.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Her mother's reply, offering a way home but asking her to wait till Diwali, helped her stay without feeling trapped.

qa.q: How might Alka's mother have felt reading that letter?
qa.a: Her mother was probably worried and missing her too, yet chose to reply calmly, leaving the door open without pulling her back.

grounding: An elder recalls homesickness and culture shock after moving, and how crying and wanting to return did not mean the move was wrong.

passage: The power went out across the hostel in Pune at nine, the week of Durga Puja, and Bidisha lay on her bed in the dark with her phone at eleven percent. Back in Kolkata, her family would be at the pandal right now, her Thakuma in her white-and-red saree, her cousins arguing over rolls. Here, nobody had even heard of the sweet she had searched three markets for. Her classmates were friendly, but no one knew that she hated coriander or that she sang when she was nervous. She felt like a guest in her own life. She tried to call home, but the network dropped twice. She started crying quietly, then harder. Her roommate Shalini sat up in the dark. "Homesick?" Bidisha nodded, then realised Shalini couldn't see. "Yes." "Me too, last year. It passes. It doesn't mean you shouldn't have come."

qa.q: What was Bidisha's phone battery at when the power went out?
qa.a: Her phone was at eleven percent.

qa.q: What is Bidisha feeling as she lies in the dark?
qa.a: Bidisha feels homesick and sad, missing her family at the pandal and feeling like an outsider where no one knows her.

qa.q: What could help Bidisha after this night?
qa.a: Talking more with Shalini, planning a proper call home, and finding a small local puja gathering could help her feel less alone without deciding the move was wrong.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel hearing Bidisha cry?
qa.a: Shalini probably feels sympathetic, remembering that same homesickness from last year, and wants Bidisha to know the feeling passes.

grounding: Shows a young adult weeks after a move missing family, food and being known, crying at night, and hearing that this does not mean the move was wrong.
